history.heading: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania
paragraphs: Baltic tribes lived in the region for thousands of years. Mindaugas united Lithuanian lands and was crowned king in 1253. Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe, officially converting to Christianity in 1387.

Under Grand Dukes such as Gediminas and Vytautas the Great, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania became one of the largest states in Europe in the 14th and 15th centuries, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea. A dynastic union with Poland in 1386 led to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569, which adopted one of the world's first written constitutions in 1791.

history.heading: Russian rule and independence
paragraphs: The partitions of the Commonwealth gave most of Lithuania to the Russian Empire in 1795. After uprisings, Russia banned the Lithuanian press in Latin letters from 1864 to 1904; books were smuggled by "book carriers".

Lithuania declared independence on 16 February 1918. Vilnius was seized by Poland in 1920, and Kaunas served as the temporary capital. In 1940 the Soviet Union occupied Lithuania; Nazi Germany occupied it from 1941 to 1944, and around 95 percent of Lithuania's large Jewish community was murdered. Soviet reoccupation brought deportations and a guerrilla resistance lasting into the 1950s.

history.heading: Restored independence
paragraphs: On 11 March 1990, Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence. Soviet troops killed 14 civilians defending the Vilnius TV tower in January 1991, but independence was recognised later that year. Lithuania joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2015.

culture.heading: Language and traditions
paragraphs: Lithuanian is one of the oldest surviving Indo-European languages, preserving many ancient features. Most Lithuanians are Catholic, and pagan traditions survive in folk customs. The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai is a famous pilgrimage site.

Vilnius's Baroque Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Food includes cepelinai (potato dumplings), šaltibarščiai (cold pink beet soup) and rye bread. Basketball is almost a religion, and Lithuania has won three Olympic bronze medals and three European championships.

politics.heading: Semi-presidential republic
paragraphs: Lithuania is a semi-presidential republic. The directly elected president leads foreign and defence policy, while the prime minister leads the government, responsible to the Seimas (parliament). Coalitions are common.

Lithuania is a strong supporter of Ukraine and has substantially increased defence spending; a German army brigade is being permanently stationed there. It allowed Taiwan to open a representative office under its own name, causing a dispute with China.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Lithuania has a high-income economy that grew rapidly after EU accession. Key sectors include manufacturing (furniture, chemicals, lasers, where it is a niche leader), food processing, logistics, financial technology and IT services. The Klaipėda LNG terminal ended its dependence on Russian gas.
Emigration has reduced the population, though many have returned in recent years. The currency is the euro.
